prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Two people, Asha and Ben, have never met. They want to agree on a secret number that only they know, but the only way to reach each other is a line that a third person, Eve, can listen to. Everything either of them says, Eve hears. For most of history this looked impossible. People who wanted a shared secret had to meet first, or send a courier carrying a codebook. In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, with help from Ralph Merkle, published a method that needs no such meeting. Mathematicians at GCHQ, the British government's signals agency, had found the same idea a few years earlier, but that work stayed classified until 1997. The method is called Diffie-Hellman key exchange, and a version of it runs every time your phone or browser opens a secure connection.

It depends on a kind of calculation that is quick to do forwards and very slow to undo. To see one, you need clock arithmetic. On a 12-hour clock, 5 hours after 9 o'clock is 2 o'clock, because 9 plus 5 is 14 and the clock starts again after 12. We can build a clock with 23 positions, numbered 0 to 22, and the rule is the same: after 22 comes 0. To find where any number lands, divide it by 23 and keep the remainder. The number 30 lands on 7. The number 50 lands on 4, because two lots of 23 make 46 and 4 is left over.

Now take powers of 5. 5 times 5 is 25, which lands on 2. Multiply by 5 again and you get 10. Again and you get 50, which lands on 4. Carrying on, the first fifteen results are 5, 2, 10, 4, 20, 8, 17, 16, 11, 9, 22, 18, 21, 13 and 19. Nothing in that list looks regular. Each entry is quick to produce, because one step gives the next. But if I told you only that some power of 5 landed on 13 and asked which one, you would have to go through the list from the start until you found it. With 23 positions that takes a minute. With a clock whose number of positions is 600 digits long, it cannot be done.

Here is the exchange. Asha and Ben first agree, in the open, on two numbers: 23 for the size of the clock and 5 for the number to take powers of. Eve hears both, and it does not matter. Asha then picks a number privately, say 6, and tells nobody. Ben picks 15 and tells nobody. Asha works out 5 to the power 6 on the clock, which is 8, and sends 8 to Ben. Ben works out 5 to the power 15, which is 19, and sends 19 to Asha. These two sent numbers are called public keys, because anyone may see them. The 6 and the 15 are private keys. Now Asha takes the 19 she received and raises it to her private power, 6. The result lands on 2. Ben takes the 8 he received and raises it to his private power, 15, and his result also lands on 2. The shared secret is 2.

They agree because of how powers combine. Ben's number is 5 to the 15th, and Asha raises it to the 6th, which gives 5 to the power of 15 times 6, or 90. Ben's route gives 5 to the power of 6 times 15, which is also 90. The order of the multiplication does not matter, so both end up at the same place, and reducing to the clock at each step does not change where the final result lands. Neither of them sent the secret. Each sent only a number that hides their private choice, and each then combined the other's number with that choice.

Eve has heard 23, 5, 8 and 19. To reach 2 she needs 6 or 15. She can find 6 by working through the list of powers of 5 until she reaches 8, and with a clock this small she would have the answer in a minute. Real systems use a clock whose size is a prime of about 600 digits, and private numbers of similar length. The list of possible powers is then far too long to search one by one, even with every computer on Earth working for longer than the universe has existed. The task of recovering the private number is called the discrete logarithm problem. No one has published a fast way to solve it in general, though nobody has proved that none exists. That is the current state of knowledge, and the security of the method rests on it.

You may wonder how Asha can compute a power of that size herself. She does not multiply 5 by itself that many times. She squares the number, squares the result, and so on, which doubles the power at each step, and then combines a few of those results. A power with 2,000 binary digits takes around 2,000 squarings, which a phone does in a fraction of a second. So the honest users do a small amount of work, and the listener faces an enormous one.

Diffie and Hellman's method produces a secret that both sides help to make. A year later, in 1977, Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman published RSA, which works differently. A person publishes a public key built from the product of two large primes, and anyone can use it to lock a message that only the holder of the primes can unlock. Multiplying two primes of 300 digits each is easy, and recovering them from the product is not. The two methods share the same shape: a public part that anyone may see, and a private part that never leaves its owner.

There is a weakness in what I have described. Eve was only listening. If she can also change what passes along the line, she can pretend to be Ben to Asha and Asha to Ben, run one exchange with each, and sit in the middle reading everything. The exchange alone does not tell Asha who is at the other end. Real systems close this gap with digital signatures, which use the same kind of public and private arithmetic to show that a public key belongs to a named party, such as your bank's website. Once the secret is agreed, both sides use it as the key for a faster cipher such as AES, which scrambles the actual data. The slow arithmetic is only used at the start.

My own view is that the surprising part is not the sums, which a school pupil can follow, but that showing the public numbers to everyone does no harm. The secret is never sent. It is built at each end from one private number and one public one.
